also: are you out of your mind?
I was out of my mind when

evidence: Hor. S. 2.6.29: quid tibi vīs, īnsāne?
terms.comment: Unsound in mind, and in talk of anyone behaving wildly: “you madman!”. The verb īnsāniō, īnsānīre is to be mad, to act crazily; īnsānia is madness.

evidence: Cic. N.D. 1.94: dēsipere, dēlīrāre, dēmentēs esse (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Very common in Cicero, of a mind gone or a senseless act.
From dē līrā, out of the furrow; of an old man in his dotage, or anyone talking nonsense. The verb is dēlīrō.
Of a crazed brain. To be crazy about someone is dēperīre (Traupman 96: eam dēperit).

terms.gloss: are you quite all there? are you mad?
terms.comment: Satin' is satisne clipped: “are you sane enough?”
Traupman’s phrase, of classical words; not found as a phrase in Lewis & Short or the loci.

terms.gloss: go mad, be out of one’s mind
terms.grammar: passive of aliēnāre, with the ablative mente
evidence: Plin. NH 28.93: aliēnārī mente, to be insane (Lewis & Short s.v. aliēnō)
Traupman 103: to go mad, mente aliēnārī
terms.comment: Literally “to be estranged from one’s mind”. Lewis & Short: the sense “drive mad” is not found before the Augustan age; the participle is the usual form, mente aliēnātus, out of his mind.

evidence: Traupman 103: he’s out of his mind, aliēnātus est ā sē
Traupman 104: he’s nuts, aliēnātus est ā sē
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase. Lewis & Short has aliēnātus mente and aliēnātus sēnsibus (Liv. 25.39) for madness, but not ā sē, which classically would mean “estranged from himself”; mente aliēnātus est says the same thing in attested words.

terms.gloss: be crazy, talk nonsense; you’re nuts!
evidence: Cic. N. D. 1.94: dēsipere, dēlīrāre, dēmentēs esse (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally “to go out of the furrow” (līra). To someone talking nonsense: Dēlīrās!.

evidence: Hor. S. 2.3.209: commōtus habēbitur (Lewis & Short s.v. commoveō, “frantic, crazed”)
terms.comment: The participle of commovēre, “stirred up”, said of a disturbed mind.
Cicero uses it to explain the ordinary word for madness, īnsānia.

terms.gloss: out of one’s mind (of a person)
evidence: Cic. Cat. 3: quis potest esse tam mente captus, quī neget? (Lewis & Short s.v. quī, cited as Cat. 3, 9)

terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Augustus apud Suet.
evidence: Suet. Aug. 87: Augustus’ word for stultus (Lewis & Short)

phrases.english: what do you want, you madman?
since you want to be crazy
whatever madness the kings commit, it is the Greeks who pay

phrases.latin: Age, dā veniam fīliō. — Satin' sānus es?
phrases.english: Come on, forgive the boy. — Are you quite all there?

phrases.latin: Dēsipiēbam mentis cum illa scrīpta mittēbam tibi.
phrases.english: I was out of my mind when I sent you that letter.
he has friends who are mere triflers
